sections.h2: How Colorado property tax is calculated
sections.html:
Three numbers make the bill. First the assessor estimates what the property is actually worth. Then a rate that depends on the property's class converts that into assessed value. Finally every taxing body that covers the parcel applies its own levy, and the levies are added together. One mill equals a tenth of a cent, which is why 13.980 mills appears as 0.013980.

Use on January 1 decides the class. Houses are valued by the market approach alone, which means recent comparable sales. Commercial and personal property can also be valued by what it costs to replace or what income it produces.

sections.h2: Who does what: assessor, taxing districts, treasurer
sections.html:
Different offices handle valuation, rates and collection, so a seller may need to call more than one number.

  • Assessor: locates, classifies and values every parcel, mails the valuation notices and rules on protests.
  • Taxing authorities: county commissioners, city councils, school boards and special district boards each decide the revenue they need and set a levy to raise it.
  • Board of equalization: the county body that hears appeals of assessor decisions.
  • Higher appeals: arbitrators, district court or the Board of Assessment Appeals take cases from the county board.
  • Treasurer: mails the statement and takes payment. El Paso County sends statements to the owner of record on the tax roll, and a statement that never arrives is no excuse for paying late.

With 64 counties there are 64 assessors and 64 treasurers, and Denver and Broomfield run city and county government together. Call the offices for the county where the house sits.

Each class of property has its own assessment rate, and houses get the lowest. In 2026 a residential parcel is assessed at 6.8% for local government levies and 7.05% for school districts.

Classification (2026)Assessment rate
Residential, local government6.8%
Residential, schools7.05%
Vacant land26%
Commercial improved25%
Commercial other26%
Industrial26%
Agricultural25%
State assessed26%

Owners of vacant lots, or of rentals the assessor treats as commercial, should check the class printed on the notice of valuation. A wrong class means a wrong rate and a bigger bill.

Real property gets a new valuation in odd-numbered years only, while personal property is revalued yearly. Notices of valuation for real property go out by May 1.

Values for tax years 2025 and 2026 come from sales between January 1, 2023 and June 30, 2024, and the state permits earlier six-month windows where sales are scarce. El Paso County applies its 2025 values to tax year 2026 using a 2023 base year, and in even-numbered years it mails notices only to parcels that changed.

Because of that lag, the price in your contract does not set the buyer's bill. The assessor's value does, and a price far above or below it changes nothing until the next reappraisal.

Statements are mailed soon after January 1. Owners choose between one payment by April 30 and two halves, due the last day of February and June 15. The split is not available on a bill of $25 or less, which is due in full by April 30.

Treasurers enforce these dates county by county. In El Paso County late payments accrue 1% interest per month, with no grace period and no partial payments, and anything still unpaid after June 15 is delinquent. From September 30 on, the office takes only cash or certified funds, with no personal checks and no postmark credit.

Colorado collects unpaid real estate tax by selling a tax lien, not the deed. El Paso County holds that sale every fall, online through RealAuction. The treasurer can tell you how long the redemption period lasts afterward.

The path begins at the assessor's office, moves to the county board of equalization, and can end at the Board of Assessment Appeals, district court or binding arbitration. El Paso County posts its calendar, so it works as a model.

  • At the assessor: file between May 1 and June 8 and expect a Notice of Determination by August 15.
  • At the board of equalization: hearings take place over Teams in July and August, and the real property protest date is in mid July.
  • At the hearing: you and the assessor get 10 minutes each, and you must prove the value you claim.
  • After the hearing: a written decision comes within five business days.
  • Further appeal: file within 30 days of the postmark on the board's decision.

Evidence must be market data from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024 for the 2025 and 2026 values. Repair estimates, an independent appraisal and photos of conditions that pull value down all count. Other counties run on different forms and dates, so read your own assessor's notice.

Three programs matter most: the senior exemption, the disabled veteran exemption and the senior deferral. The senior exemption takes half of the first $200,000 of a primary residence's actual value off the tax base, if the state funds it. Applicants must be 65 or older and have owned and lived in the home for 10 years in a row, and the assessor wants the form by July 15.

  • Veteran with a disability and Gold Star spouse: the same 50% of the first $200,000, with a July 1 filing date.
  • Qualified senior primary residence classification: covers tax years 2025 and 2026 for former exemption holders who moved, with a March 15 filing date.
  • Senior deferral: open to anyone 65 or older who applies with the county treasurer from January 1 to April 1, and it has to be renewed yearly.

The state treasurer effectively lends the deferred amount and records a lien. The loan comes due on a sale or transfer of title, and also on death, on a move for reasons other than health, or when the home is rented. A seller with a deferral should order a payoff figure before closing.

sections.h2: Why equal homes get different bills
sections.html:
Levies differ by district, and every house belongs to its own mix. The El Paso County list for tax year 2025, billed in 2026, runs from 2.938 mills for Pikes Peak Library District and 3.009 for the City of Colorado Springs, through 6.857 for the county, up to school districts at 37.695 (Colorado Springs District 11), 45.459 (Academy District 20) and 57.682 (Widefield District 3).

Two houses a few miles apart can land in different school and fire districts and pay different totals, and metro districts in newer subdivisions add still more. Your own tax statement lists the entities that apply.

Before signing, have the title company report where this year's taxes stand. The treasurer bills whoever is the owner of record, and some mortgage servicers collect taxes in escrow while others do not, so ask your lender which applies.

Hail and wildfire damage can lower what a buyer will pay. An owner behind on tax with a damaged roof can ask for an as is cash offer instead of paying for repairs first, and closing then pays the back tax out of the proceeds.

faqs.q: What is the Colorado property tax due date?
faqs.a: Pay by April 30 in one payment, or split it into halves due the last day of February and June 15. A bill of $25 or less must be paid whole by April 30.

faqs.q: How often does Colorado reassess property?
faqs.a: Real property is revalued in odd-numbered years and notices go out by May 1, while personal property is revalued every year.

faqs.q: What interest applies to late Colorado property tax?
faqs.a: The county decides. El Paso County charges 1% per month from the first day late, and taxes unpaid after June 15 are delinquent.

faqs.q: Can I get a property tax break as a Colorado senior?
faqs.a: Possibly. Owners 65 or older who have lived in and owned the home 10 years running can have half of the first $200,000 of actual value exempted, if the state funds it. Apply to the county assessor by July 15.

faqs.q: What happens to a senior tax deferral when I sell?
faqs.a: The deferral comes due on a sale or title transfer. Because the deferred tax and interest sit as a lien, closing pays them out of your proceeds.
